records.title: Show HN: Interview your analysts instead of auto-generating a semantic layer
records.author: ronpotok
records.storyText:
I’ve spent the last year building context for AI analysts in the mid-market. I’ve open sourced a library from my learnings, along the same principles of the Matt Pocock skills.

Principles:

* Claude / Codex / Cursor etc are great data agents - you just need context to enable them to answer business questions correctly.

* Much of the important context lives in analysts heads'

* Context must be maintainable (short, human readable - markdown and yaml)

* Added context should be load bearing, not repeat of information that is available in another source of truth - and evaluations prove the value of the context

* Companies should own their own context, and must be shareable with any model

* Context should be version controlled (and github works as a context store).

What the library does:

* Performs an interview with your analysts (context-interview skill), one domain at a time, similar to what I have done as a consultant. The interview is informed by your query logs.

* The AI develops evaluation questions at the same time as building the context - and at the end of each domain interview asks you to run an evaluation with and without the context. The evaluation will actually check the results against your dashboards if you allow it. We have shown increases in accuracy from 87% to 95% by adding this context in our imaginary open-source company, Shorelane.

* Provides a set of skills to use the context that follow best practices for self service analytics:

  * Write a plain english plan for the business user to approve

  * Execute the plan

  * Verify that the execution followed the plan, and provide a simple uncertainty score. 

  * Enable a adversarial review of the answer if their are doubts.
What you get:

Context repo written in markdown and yaml after you finish the interview. We use a single github repo, divided into domains. The interview can be shared and restarted by checking in/out of github.

A set of skills to share with your business team

Optional: We offer a fast MCP server to serve the Github-based context to your team.

records.title: Show HN: Shop via CLI; for agents and software engineers
records.author: marram
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

We're building a single search/browse API interface to thousands of ecommerce stores (hopefully, eventually, all of them). Inspired by Shopify's https://shop.dev, we embedded a WASM bridge of our CLI in our website.

The idea is to provide an efficient commerce interface for agents; personal assistants (Instinct et al) or otherwise. The alternatives are to build a crawling system / Firecrawl, use an LLM search api (Exa, Parallel etc) or use embedded headless browsers. Collective action by brands/retailers to implement agentic-protocols (UCP, ACP etc) is unlikely; so we're doing it for them.

Surprisingly, despite our coverage list being smaller than Shopify's and the search endpoint being slower (~3k ms for p90; because there is JEV and/or LLM to convert free form search to facets) the search results are often subjectively better:

``` storerouter search 'gold frame pink tint sunglasses' --facet category_path.depth_3=sunglasses --facet temple_color=gold --facet lens_color=pink --facet eyewear_frame_material=metal ```

vs Shop.dev's: ``` shop search 'gold frame pink tint sunglasses' --category gid://shopify/TaxonomyCategory/aa-2-27 # dropped facet temple_color=temple_color__gold (no Shopify filter) # dropped facet lens_color=lens_color__pink (no Shopify filter) # dropped facet eyewear_frame_material=eyewear_frame_material__metal (no Shopify filter) # category 'sunglasses' → Apparel & Accessories > Clothing Accessories > Sunglasses ```

records.title: Show HN: Weir - Catch credential leaks in the AI agents you build and use
records.author: CodeNinja778
records.storyText:
Hi HN. Weir is for one problem: credentials crossing the boundaries of your AI agent.

For agents you build, Weir plants fake credentials where real ones would live, runs the agent's normal flows, and checks what comes out: telemetry, logs, console output, model requests, and requests to other services. It looks for those exact values, including common encoded forms, and reports where they went without printing the credential.

pip install weir-scan weir canary judge --sample

That sample shows a planted key leaking into a trace. On your own agent: pip install weir-run.

For agents you use, Weir can inventory your real credentials (it stores keyed fingerprints, never the values) and show when one enters your session or leaves in a tool call. Right now, this is supported for Claude Code. Its optional hook redacts those known credentials from tool results before the model sees them. Setup is weir statusline setup, on Linux and macOS for now.

So the two modes are deliberately different:

Build: plant → run → prove where the credential went. Use: observe → warn → optionally redact before the model sees it.

The test mode is deterministic and offline. On Linux it can also run the agent without outside network access, so direct exfiltration attempts are caught. If a required path wasn't exercised, Weir reports incomplete, never clean.

It doesn't try to detect every possible secret. It matches known whole values, so hashed, split, truncated, or otherwise transformed credentials aren't covered. The Claude Code hook only protects the tool-result boundary: it can't undo a credential already pasted into the conversation, and a failed command's output reaches the model as is.

Apache-2.0, no model in the loop, and Weir itself sends nothing anywhere. It found GHSA-j7qq-vr8c-xvw3 in MLflow (fixed in 3.17.0).

Built with AI assistance; every security finding was reproduced before I reported it.

records.title: Show HN: Formstep, Request information from customers without the back-and-forth
records.author: mellosty
records.storyText:
I built Formstep: https://formstep.io

The idea came from a problem I kept running into while working on loan applications.

A workflow could automate a large part of the process, but eventually it would need something only the customer could provide: a document, a correction, a signature, an explanation, or confirmation of some information.

At that point, workflow automation basically did not work.

The forms themselves were also often the source of the problem. Applications came in with wrong documents, misunderstood questions, incomplete answers, or people simply forgetting to finish.

Someone had to email the customer, explain what was missing, wait for a reply then follow up again. It was always back-and-forth.

So I built Formstep to make requesting information from customers easier, not only for humans, but also for workflows and AI agents.

The idea is: A person, workflow, or AI agent sends a customer a request through email or a link. Either re-use existing form or create unique for each customer.

You can prefill what you already know, lock fields, pass context, and only ask the customer what you need.

For example, we might already know:

* Address that you already have in the CRM

* Company description from the internet

* What a agreement document must contain

* How a good answer should be

Formstep can check inputs and uploaded files while the customer is filling out the form and tell them if something is missing or inconsistent before they submit. For example “The PDF does not contain your signature” or “Invoice total does not match the order amount”.

The goal is to catch problems while the customer is still there, rather than letting bad data continue through the workflow and discovering it later.

On the automation side, requests can currently be created through n8n, Zapier, the REST API, or by an AI agent over MCP. When the customer finishes, the structured answers can go back into the workflow so it can continue.

Forms and invitation/reminder are multilingual, and submitted answers can be translated inside the dashboard with one click. If you want, Formstep can be used as normal form builder and shared through public links, QR, embeds etc. It support custom themes for dark/light mode, with cover image, has Notion-style editor and much more. The list is too long to fit here.

I want to make Formstep a plattform where it becomes more intelligent over time and ensures that we can get better answers from customers for any use case.

My question to you: Where do your automations currently stop because they need input from a customer or user, and how are you handling that today?

If you are interested in trying out the n8n node: https://www.npmjs.com/package/n8n-nodes-formstep

Zapier integration: https://zapier.com/apps/formstep/integrations

Connecting your AI agent: https://docs.formstep.io/developers/mcp-server/

Docs: https://docs.formstep.io

I would love your feedback and please try a quick demo at https://app.formstep.io/try

records.title: Show HN: SnapFire FSR: Full Stack Web Apps Served via Rust IR Engine
records.author: excsn
records.storyText:
SnapFire FSR is a full stack runtime that lets frontend teams write typescript and have it served via Rust.

At my current workplace (10M+ DAUs), all we want to do was render composed strings from the backend to a browser using Typescript. Since Node 0.x (went I started with Node), things have changed, freedoms taken away and now security teams recommend to wrap your Node server instance with a sidecar or else your Node project will be blocked. SnapFire FSR changes that for us, no more sidecars.

The idea is, you don't need a general purpose VM to compose a web page. Most complex transformations and communications are done by our services anyway. When you need complex computation done without a service then create native Rust functions and call it via Typescript.

There is a long list of ideas from my past experience with frontend and backend that contributed to SnapFire FSR. In the end, FSR answers my question "Can we specialize our web applications to our full stack needs and security concerns?"

records.title: Show HN: Instance – A clean-room reimplementation of GameMaker 8.1 in Rust
records.author: __grob
records.storyText:
I used GameMaker 8.1 a ton in late elementary and middle school, and GML was the first programming language I wrote. I still think it's a fun engine to use because it has so many batteries included. So I built an open-source reimplementation of it in Rust which I'm calling Instance. It opens existing .gmk and .gm81 projects and runs them on Windows, macOS and in the browser, with a more efficient GML interpreter than the original GameMaker.

You can try the IDE here in your browser: https://groverburger.github.io/instance/. It comes with three example games, including Spelunky Classic built from Derek Yu's released source shared under its permissive license. Just change something and press Run to see your edits in action.

Old GM games depend on a lot of quirks such as the order events run in, the exact random number generator, how sound_isplaying lags behind the audio. I wrote up the behavior as specs from the documentation, the file formats and black-box tests against the real program, then implemented it from those specs. No proprietary code was disassembled or decompiled. CLEANROOM.md describes the process.

It covers most of almost all of 8.1. All the resource editors, GML and drag-and-drop actions, d3d, particles, surfaces, MIDI, mplay multiplayer and DLL calls. It can also export a game as a standalone executable or a single HTML file. Projects can be saved as folders of plain text and PNG files for git.

I wrote most of the code with Claude Opus 5.5 over about three weeks. Claude banged out a pretty good reimplementation in a morning, but as always the last 20% took 80% of the work. GameMaker also turns out to work surprisingly well with LLMs. GML is small and simple, and a whole game fits in one project file.

I'm happy to answer any questions!

Code: https://github.com/groverburger/instance

Frontier models improve at a pace faster than the pace at which most humans are able to keep up. Not all of us are obsessed with pushing the boundaries of our agents and trying new ways to work with them. records.title: Show HN: Algeon – Compose GPU graph, vector, and ML algorithms in SQL
records.author: morristai
records.storyText:
Algeon is a query engine built on Apache DataFusion that exposes NVIDIA's cuGraph, cuVS, and cuML as SQL table functions. It doesn't write its GPU kernels. Instead, it takes what NVIDIA already has and embeds it into DataFusion, so you can call those GPU operations on any arbitrary data, with filter/join/agg using plain SQL.

And why would you want that? Because GPU analytics used to require ad-hoc ETL pipelines, Python glue code, and imperative operation calls. That makes it hard to fit into a backend API service, and it isn't flexible enough for frequent exploratory iteration, adapting to different search conditions and data. Think of agents trying to answer complex questions on a datalake, which involves not only relational operations, but also graph/vector/ML analytics. They can now use declarative SQL to test their hypotheses and build the next query based on the previous response, making GPU OLAP an interactive service. Algeon can also be used as a library living inside your backend service, so your query response can be used directly within a single process, saving the transfer cost between the query engine and backend service.

I started building Algeon last year. At first, it was cuDF Rust FFI bindings that aimed to bring GPU ETL pipelines into a single backend process, and it worked very well. Then I realized it might be possible to move GPU data science workloads into an OLAP query engine, since the NVIDIA RAPIDS ecosystem and DataFusion are mature.

For use cases, architecture design, benchmarks, and more, feel free to check out, any feedback is welcome https://algeon.dev/

records.author: scronkfinkle

This is a project I've been working on for about 8 months now. I worked in legal tech for 3 years and found that one of the biggest hurdles for AI agents and lawyers alike when doing legal research is tracking changes, and correctly cross referencing those changes between different forms of legal documents.

W2D builds a SQLite dataset from public sources, and offers agent skills for answering questions about that dataset.

The dataset holds multiple revisions of the U.S. Code at each release point that you add. It holds the public laws that amend the Code, and it links each amendment to the change that it made. It holds court opinions from CourtListener, by page and paragraph, and it links each U.S.C. citation to the provision that the court cited. It can also hold House roll calls.

This is similar in spirit to "git for Law" but includes a lot more utilities than diffs to make it an effective tool for research.

records.title: Show HN: Crulon – Business phone where AI does the work, humans make the calls
records.author: rayn11
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Rayhan. Crulon is a business phone system where an AI agent answers the line and your team works alongside it. You can talk with our demo agent right in your browser, no sign-up: https://crulon.ai/#talk

Why I built it: I’ve spent eight years as a software and network engineer, mostly building tools for internet providers, and kept watching small support teams lose customers in the seams. Calls missed after hours. Calls passed from a bot to a person who had to start over. Most voice AI products are a bot sitting on someone else’s phone line, so a handoff means forwarding to another number and losing the context. We built the phone system and the agent as one thing.

What that gets you:

The handoff happens inside the same system. When something isn’t the AI’s job, it asks the caller, then rings your team (in the browser or on a desk phone) with a note on why they’re calling. Live calls: anyone with permission can listen to an AI call (no one on the call can hear them) and take it over. It’s the same call, with no transfer and no hold music; the AI just leaves. Tools: the agent can call any API you define in an Action builder (look up the caller, open a ticket), and it checks with the caller before changing anything. Outbound campaigns: the agent works through a call list for reminders, renewals and follow-ups, and puts interested people through to your team. SIP desk phones, and bring-your-own-carrier so you can keep your numbers. If you run out of AI minutes, calls follow your fallback route (ring the team, voicemail) instead of dropping, and the refused call isn’t billed.

How it’s built, briefly: calls come in over SIP into Call Flows (menus, queues, schedules), and your team answers in the browser or on SIP desk phones. Each agent runs on one of two engines. Classic transcribes, thinks, then speaks, so you get exact wording and English, Spanish and French. Live is a full-duplex speech model that listens while it talks and hands tool work to a second model. One fun problem with that split was teaching the agent when to hang up, which I wrote up here: https://crulon.ai/blog/teaching-a-voice-agent-to-hang-up

It isn’t a CRM; it works alongside yours. Built-in Apps connect it to systems like billing and network tools, and anything with a web API plugs in through the Action builder.

Pricing is per seat ($24, $49 or $89 a month) with a pool of AI minutes; human calls are included. If you sign up this month, HN30 takes 30% off the first 3 months.

I’ll be here all day. Try the agent, try to trip it up, and tell me what you’d want from a phone system like this.

records.title: Show HN: Aigent-OS, a Claude Code harness that clears and resumes
records.author: wrg32786
records.storyText:
I run my business on four Claude Code agents: Titus, Pheme, Davinci and Metis. They write my newsletter, The AIgent (about 9k subscribers), every day through a drafting and proofreading engine that Pheme checks before scheduling. They also build AI courses, run a pipeline that turns the day's featured repo into a talking-head video of my avatar for Instagram, set up ad deals, and run Meta ads and email funnels with me. Nothing closes until I sign off. Metis posts jobs on a job board and the others claim them.
The hard part wasn't any single task. It was keeping the agents coherent over weeks. Compaction kept dropping the small decisions, and then an agent would redo work I'd already ruled out.
aigent-os is my fix. At a context threshold (80% by default) the agent writes a capsule, a checkpoint file in git, and has to reply with one exact line. Only then does the runner send /clear, wait for a SessionStart receipt proving a fresh session started, and resume. One ack buys at most one clear. If anything is ambiguous it stops at HOLD:clear-stalled-after-ack and doesn't retry. On resume the capsule is reference only, live state wins, and anything the writer couldn't capture is written as Unknown. First run interviews you with three plain questions and makes a first plan. Each agent gets its own memory vault.
Limits, honestly: the public evidence is 11 of 11 cycles on one Windows seat. The runner can still miss a permission dialog (#104), a seat launched from inside another Claude Code session can lose its transcript (#98), and scrolling the seat window sends stray input (#99). v1.1.0 shipped on Sunday.
Try bash install.sh --dry-run, it writes nothing. I'd like to hear where the loop could still double clear or strand a session.

records.title: Show HN: Muscle Memory – Can you still write code without AI?
records.author: ekkuleivonen
records.storyText:
Developer of 6 years here, been using AI (increasingly) over the last year for most of my work. A few weeks back I started to look for new jobs as the current startup I work for is falling into pieces. "Do I need to do leetcode again?" - I thought. So I picked a few challenges and tried to solve them without an assistant.

This felt impossible. What?! Is this the brainrot everyone is talking about? I mean I still read code every day, I just don't write it anymore. I could read and review the solution easily, but writing it myself felt like speaking a language I only understand, but cannot speak.

Being the data hoarder I am, I immediately wanted numbers, so I built Muscle Memory to help me feed them.

It's like leetcode but better. Challenges are more realistic, and I'd like to think the UX is more straightforward. It covers 12 languages and your code runs in a network-denied sandbox in your browser. No account needed.

I want it to be a place to keep your hands sharp: short tasks, clear prompts, and difficulty that comes from solving the problem rather than figuring out what the question means.

About the data (that I'm curious about): With your consent, Muscle Memory records your practice as raw events, including keystrokes, runs and submissions. Hoping to build an open dataset of how we write code in the AI era. That could help us understand how we approach problems, where we get stuck, and how we well do we retain our craft during this transition.

Your individual results stay private unless you share them. “Stealth” mode keeps your data out of published findings, and you can export or delete everything.

The data will be published as a report/notebook on the site itself, and be available raw under MIT license (parquet) once we reach a critical mass of sorts, so it makes sense to share.

The code is also MIT-licensed on GitHub (https://github.com/ekkuleivonen/muscle-memory). I wrote more about why I built it in the manifesto here: https://musclememory.run/manifesto.

I'd especially like to hear what surprised you about your first attempt.

Try it out here: https://musclememory.run

records.title: Show HN: Shufler: 3D gaming harness around your coding harness and dev pipeline
records.author: jgrichardson67
records.storyText:
Hi HN. Greg here.

I've been a full stack engineer for 20 years. Now all I do is shuffle messages between users, my agent fleet, our dev pipeline.. back and forth. I miss coding, solving problems, reasoning, and having an understanding and a mental model of all the work I'm juggling. But this is the job now, and there's no going back. I don't exactly feel like a 10x engineer yet, but I am for sure a 10-tab engineer.

I built (er, Claude built) Shufler to lean into my new reality. If the job is basically to shuffle things through a pipeline, why not have it be more fun.

Each row on the 3D gameboard is one of your existing terminal sessions. The columns are the steps your work moves through: Brainstorm, Plan, Build, QA, Review, Merge, Deploy. Your shipped PRs get stored in a warehouse/depot. The main things flowing across the board are your issues and PRs: each one rides along its session/row as it moves through review, CI and merge, and anything waiting on you turns red. I tend to manage several PRs within each Claude/Codex session, and this makes it easier for me to hold onto a mental model of where everything is. It's also made daily standups much easier to read-out.

I created a few skins/themes like a casino, a theme park, sky islands, a starship and a factory, because.. of course.

MacOS, works with Claude Code and Codex CLI, and cmux and iTerm (tmux should work, but I haven't tested it). It doesn't try to replace anything you already use.. just makes the orchestration more fun. You can still shift focus over to your terminal sessions when needed, use your existing skills, MCP servers, etc. There's a 3D library-building in each skin where you can specify your markdown/context folders or files, and then drag and drop to check them out by your rows/sessions.

I tried to be thoughtful on security, following patterns that I consider at work. No telemetry, and the only outside calls are your own gh calls to GitHub. Daemon only listens on localhost, and every action shows its command before it runs. MCP server is opt-in, and sending to other sessions is off by default; if you turn it on, every send is a preview plus a separate confirm you approve. Details are in the README's #safety-and-privacy, and the MCP threat model (including what it doesn't protect against) is in docs/MCP.md. To report a security issue privately (or contributions to improve), see SECURITY.md.

Demo with mock data, nothing to install at https://shufler.app

Repo at https://github.com/jgrichardson/shufler (MIT)

records.title: Show HN: DocPerRow – one Word document per spreadsheet row, in the browser
records.author: Artem_Trofy
records.storyText:
I built this after reading a lot of threads from people fighting Word's mail merge: Word for the web doesn't have it at all, and desktop Word's "Finish & Merge" gives you one long document rather than a separate, sensibly named file per record. The usual workarounds are VBA macros, Graham Mayor's add-in (Windows desktop only), or Google Docs add-ons that need your data in Drive.

DocPerRow does it client-side: you write {Column name} placeholders in a .docx, drop in an xlsx/xls/ods/csv, pick a file-name pattern like {LastName} {InvoiceNo}, and get a ZIP with one .docx per row. It's a static site using docxtemplater, PizZip and SheetJS. Your files never leave the browser. The only outgoing requests are cookie-less GoatCounter analytics (page views and event names such as "run") and a same-origin counter that stores the event name and UI language; no file contents or names are sent.

docxtemplater already copes with Word splitting a placeholder like {Name} across several XML runs, which is what I feared most. The work went elsewhere:

- Excel date cells: the "locale default" date format is stored as m/d/yy, so dates have to be re-rendered in the user's locale or a Polish user gets 10/20/26.

- CSVs saved by Ukrainian/Polish Excel are often CP1251/CP1250, not UTF-8.

Free up to 20 documents per run, no sign-up. It outputs .docx only (no PDF yet). I'd like to hear what's missing for your use case, and whether the 20-document limit or the template syntax gets in the way.
